1 Results
As the primary goal of this paper is to provide a practical manual for building and operating the MMLab, the results of our analyses are outside the present scope. Interested readers are encouraged to visit the Results chapter of our online MMLab Quarto manual for a detailed account of the experimental findings.
Having described the MI analysis pipeline, we now present the results of this proof-of-concept experiment. As noted throughout, these results are based on a single dyad (the authors) and are not intended for formal statistical inference. To provide a conceptual framework, we consider three hypotheses that a researcher investigating interpersonal synchrony during joint singing might plausibly hold (we stress that these hypotheses are not formally tested here, they serve only as a narrative scaffold): - (H1) Vision facilitates vocal synchrony: dyads synchronize their (joint-singing) vocal amplitude envelopes more strongly when they can see each other than when visual access is blocked. - (H2) Movement further enhances vocal synchrony: vocal synchrony is highest when participants can both see each other and move freely, as co-singing gestures provide an additional coordination channel. - (H3) Vision and movement increase cross-modal physiological coupling: Beyond vocal singing synchrony, the dyad’s physiological signals (ECG, respiration, EMG) become more coupled across participants when both vision and movement are available, reflecting a broader state of interpersonal alignment. To visualize the full extent of interpersonal coupling across all modalities and conditions, we generated a network plot (Figure S10) and distribution plot (Figure S11) for each of the four experimental conditions. Figure S10. Interpersonal Multimodal Synchrony across Experimental Conditions. The four quadrants show the four experimental conditions (Movement X Vision: top-left; Movement X No_Vision: top-right; No_Movement X Vision: bottom-left; No_Movement X No_Vision: bottom-right; ). Each quadrant shows the same mutual information (MI) values in two ways. Left: coupling network. Nodes P1 (blue) are on the left and nodes for P2 (orange) are on the right. Right: cross-modality MI matrix. Columns are P1 signals (blue) and rows are P2 signals (orange). In both plots the signals appear in the same order: audio amplitude envelope, EMG bicep, EMG tricep, ECG, right-index-finger motion in the x, y and z axes, and respiration. Each of the 64 lines in the network, and each of the 64 cells in the matrix, is the MI between one P1 signal and one P2 signal. The value is the maximum MI across lags, averaged over all sliding windows and trials in that condition. Diagonal cells show within-modality coupling, and off-diagonal cells show cross-modality coupling,. The colour of lines and cells, and the thickness of lines, scale with MI strength: dark purple (min 0.0( is low MI and yellow is high MI (max 1.0). One colour bar applies to all panels. The results displayed in Figure S11 point to the following patterns: - Vocal Synchrony (H1 and H2). The within-modality Audio P1–P2 coupling (the diagonal Audio–Audio cell) was highest in the two movement conditions: NoVision × Movement (MI = 0.801) and Vision × Movement (MI = 0.787), compared to Vision × NoMovement (MI = 0.673) and NoVision × NoMovement (MI = 0.587). This pattern suggests that the freedom to move (rather than interpersonal visual access per se) was the primary driver of vocal synchrony in this dyad, only partially supporting H1 (vision facilitates vocal synchrony) but more clearly supporting H2 (movement enhances vocal synchrony). Notably, the NoVision × NoMovement condition yielded the lowest audio coupling of all four conditions, consistent with the idea that restricting both channels simultaneously most strongly impairs vocal coordination. - Physiological Coupling (H3). The heart rate coupling between participants was high across all conditions, with the highest values observed in the NoVision × Movement condition (MI = 1.018) and NoVision × NoMovement condition (MI = 0.866), followed by Vision × NoMovement (MI = 0.805) and Vision × Movement (MI = 0.717). This pattern does not directly support H3 (that vision and movement increase physiological coupling). Rather, it might suggest that cardiac synchrony in this dyad could have been driven by shared respiratory and movement entrainment, rather than by visual contact. Respiration coupling was relatively stable across conditions (ranging from 0.684 to 0.754), suggesting that the shared singing task itself was the dominant factor regardless of visual or movement manipulations. EMG coupling (both biceps and triceps) remained consistently low across all conditions (MI < 0.12). - Cross-Modality Coupling. Beyond the within-modality diagonal, the matrices reveal notable cross-modal patterns. In particular, the heart rate signal from one participant consistently showed elevated coupling with the other participant’s motion signals (e.g., Heart Rate P2 × Motion X P1 = 0.807 in Vision × Movement; 0.858 in NoVision × Movement) and respiration (Heart Rate P2 × Respiration P1 = 0.577 in Vision × Movement; 0.811 in NoVision × Movement). This cross-modal heart rate–motion–respiration cluster likely reflects the physiological interdependence of these systems during physical activity: movement drives respiration, which in turn modulates heart rate. In contrast, the EMG signals showed minimal cross-modal coupling with any other modality, remaining consistently below MI ≈ 0.30 across all conditions and pairings.
Figure Y. Coupling Network of Interpersonal Multimodal Synchrony
Note. [..4 Conditions..] Each dot represents a single MI value from one 5-second sliding window. MI values are grouped into three categories: audio envelope coupling (gold), within-modality coupling (green; same modality across participants, excluding audio), and cross-modality coupling (red; different modalities across participants). Horizontal black lines indicate the group mean for each category.
[Results for Figure Y, if we decide to keep it]
Taken together, these exploratory results illustrate that the MMLab can capture condition-dependent differences in interpersonal multimodal synchrony during a face-to-face joint singing task. The result patterns observed (i.e., stronger vocal synchrony in the Vision x Movement compared to the NoVision x No Movement conditions ) are broadly consistent with what one might expect from two participants engaged in a structured co-singing task, even though not all hypothesized patterns were confirmed (notably, movement appeared to matter more than vision for vocal synchrony, and physiological coupling did not follow the predicted Vision + Movement gradient). We emphasize, again, that these results are purely descriptive. A researcher applying this pipeline to a substantive research question would need to address several methodological considerations before drawing inferential conclusions. For instance, the large number of pairwise comparisons (64 modality pairs × 4 conditions × multiple time windows) substantially inflates the risk of false positives, and appropriate corrections for multiple testing (e.g., Bonferroni, FDR) would be essential. Additionally, it would be important to establish the chance-level coupling through surrogate analyses (e.g., comparing MI values computed on surrogate participants dyads from real-dyad MI values), as some degree of MI between two signals can arise simply from shared stationarity or slow drift, rather than from meaningful moment-to-moment coordination. Finally, the proof-of-concept presented here used a single landmark (right index finger) for the motion modality and a single summary statistic (maximum MI across lags) per window. Future work could explore richer representations of movement (e.g., full-body kinematic features) and alternative coupling measures (e.g., phase-locking value, Granger causality) to capture different facets of interpersonal coordination. [ END OF QUARTO ONLY RESULTS SECTION]

MethodsProcessing Code

1.1 Stream Extraction & Conversion
We use a custom Python script to extract the individual multimodal streams from the unified .xdf file, convert them into workable .csv files, and segment them based on the marker events timestamps.
[Quarto Link with Script and Explanation: MML_XDF_Preprocessing.ipynb]
Using the pyxdf library, the script loads and parses the .xdf files hierarchically at the meta-data level of each stream (which includes the stream’s name, type, nominal sampling rate, channel labels, and time stamps).
[CODE: 2_PREPROCESSING/1_XDF_PROCESSING/MML_XDF_Preprocessing.ipynb#xdf-load] [CODE: 2_PREPROCESSING/1_XDF_PROCESSING/MML_XDF_Preprocessing.ipynb#xdf-stream-metadata]. Because stream metadata data may vary across sessions depending on device configuration or recording order, we performed a naming standardization procedure according to the experiment-specific configuration (e.g., explicitly assigning streams to Participant 1 or Participant 2 and labeling physiological channels consistently) to ensure consistent referencing across streams. [CODE: 2_PREPROCESSING/1_XDF_PROCESSING/MML_XDF_Preprocessing.ipynb#xdf-load-rename].
Each stream is then extracted as the raw time series together with their corresponding LSL timestamps, organized into a tabular structure and exported as a workable .csv file.
Audio streams were separately converted into standard .wav files using the SciPy library at their declared sampling frequency (i.e., 16 kHz). An additional noise-reduction using the noisereduce library (Sainburg 2019) was also applied with a pre-defined stationary threshold of 1.5 to reduce background noise.
[CODE: 2_PREPROCESSING/1_XDF_PROCESSING/MML_XDF_Preprocessing.ipynb#xdf-denoise].

1.2 Stream Segmentation
In the same script, we also perform a temporal segmentation of each .csv data stream using the shared LSL timestamps of the Event Marker stream, corresponding to our experimentally relevant time boundaries (i.e., start and end trial of each condition).
[CODE: 2_PREPROCESSING/1_XDF_PROCESSING/MML_XDF_Preprocessing.ipynb#xdf-seg-markers].
This is achieved by identifying the relevant start-end pairs based on a flexible, user-defined segmentation method using the shared LSL time (e.g., full-session segmentation, condition based segmentation, trial-level segmentation, custom defined timings). The final output of this preprocessing stage was hierarchically organized into folders structured by participant ID, session number and type of segmentation, allowing for organized multimodal post-processing.
[CODE: 2_PREPROCESSING/1_XDF_PROCESSING/MML_XDF_Preprocessing.ipynb#xdf-csv-export].

1.3 Clipping Raw Videos
To align the externally saved composite videos with the rest of the LSL streams, a custom Python script clips each composite video based on the corresponding frame indices that were sent to LSL during data collection and processed into workable.csv (Section 1.3)
[Quarto Link with Script and Explanation MML_AudioVideo_Sync]
Specifically, using the first and last frame indices from each LSL .csv file (step 2.2), the script trims the corresponding raw video using OpenCV (Bradski 2000) to that exact frame range.
[CODE: 2_PREPROCESSING/2_AudioVideo_Sync/MML_AudioVideo_Sync.ipynb#video-lsl-frame-range].
Importantly, the output frame rate is calculated empirically from the LSL data (frame count divided by elapsed time) rather than taken from video metadata, since the latter may not reflect actual frame rate due to dropped frames or other irregularities during acquisition.
[CODE: 2_PREPROCESSING/2_AudioVideo_Sync/MML_AudioVideo_Sync.ipynb#video-cfr-plan].

1.4 Merging Clipped Videos with Audios
To verify that trimmed video and audio are perfectly synchronized, the same script also allows the user to merge these video-audio pairs using ffmpeg. The video stream is copied without re-encoding to preserve the original visual quality, while the audio stream is re-encoded as AAC, producing a single merged audio-video file in which the two modalities are temporally aligned according to the shared LSL timing.
[CODE: 2_PREPROCESSING/2_AudioVideo_Sync/MML_AudioVideo_Sync.ipynb#av-ffmpeg-merge]. (In case further debugging is needed due to audio-video de-synchronizations, the script includes an optional step in which the LSL timestamps and frame numbers (from the LSL .csv file) are overlaid onto each frame of the trimmed videos (which already contain a running frame counter created during recording with the MML_Video3Cameras_LSL.py script). This allows the user to visually inspect any possible mismatch between the LSL timing/frames and the native video frames) [CODE: 2_PREPROCESSING/2_AudioVideo_Sync/MML_AudioVideo_Sync.ipynb#av-overlay-lsl].
MethodsLab Setup Code

1.1 Video

1.1.1 Choosing the Video Recording Setup
The MMLab camera setup is primarily optimized for video-based, whole-body 3D motion tracking (MT). Thanks to rapid advancements in motion analysis technologies and fueled by growing interest across research and clinical domains, there are many MT systems available on the market, each offering distinct strengths and trade-offs (for a comprehensive review of different systems see van Schaik and Dominici 2020). For our MMLab setup, we opted for a video-based MT workflow (using computer-vision model for pose estimation from video recording) rather than device-based systems (which use dedicated sensors to capture movement), since it best aligns with our five core requirements. In fact, while device-based systems (e.g., Vicon or Qualysis) can reach sub-millimeter accuracy, they come at a steep financial cost (typically > €100,000 or more for full systems, see van der Kruk and Reijne 2018; van Schaik and Dominici 2020). In contrast, video-based solutions using consumer-grade cameras can be implemented for under €1,000, making them orders of magnitude more affordable. Importantly, video-based MT workflows still maintain high levels of precision that are sufficient for most behavioral studies, with acceptable loss of accuracy compared to state-of-the-art device-based systems for many tasks (for performance comparisons between video-based and device-based systems, see Koul and Novembre 2025; Martini et al. 2022; Ota et al. 2020; Pouw, Trujillo, and Dixon 2020).
Additionally, the free and open-source nature of most computer-vision models – such as OpenPose (Cao et al. 2021) or Mediapipe (Lugaresi et al. 2019) – has dramatically improved the accessibility of MT for many researches that do not have access to proprietary hardware (and their black-boxed software). Finally, in contrast to the complex, expensive-to-insure, and sometimes bulky nature of device-based motion tracking systems, video-based MT setups can consist of lightweight, and portable components (e.g., USB-cameras, foldable tripods, and a laptop). This makes them ideal for mobile research settings and, notably, particularly suitable for studying diverse populations like human infants and non-human animals, as they do not require wearable sensors or body markers (Białek et al. 2025).


1.1.2 Video-Recording Equipment Specs
The video-recording setup of MMLab comprises six USB cameras mounted on two movable arches, with three cameras assigned to (i.e., facing) each participant. Each triplet of cameras was connected to a dedicated recording computer (Dell Precision 3640 Tower) to manage the video streams independently for each participant. To improve portability, the camera arches can be replaced with foldable tripods provided that each camera remains fixed during recording and positioned approximately at the participants’ head height across all sessions. Although a single front-facing camera is sufficient for basic 2D body pose estimation, using three simultaneous viewpoints allows for triangulation in 3D space (i.e., pose estimation includes depth dimension). For the cameras, here we chose the Elgato Facecam (model: Full HD). Each unit is relatively inexpensive (~€120), lightweight (96 g), capable of recording in full-HD resolution (1080p) at 60 Hz, and comes with free software (Elgato Camera Hub) that allows for adjusting camera settings. Crucially, the cameras have modifiable shutter speeds (up to 1/250s), which is an important component for motion tracking, as lower shutter speeds (below 1/100s) tend to introduce motion blur that can impair pose estimation accuracy (see Supplementary Material, section X). Naturally, other camera models can be utilized, as long as they allow for shutter speeds above 1/100s.
[ Quarto only: Supplementary Materials Section 1 See here for shutter speed analyses. ] In video recording, shutter speed refers to the length of time the camera captures light in each frame and is typically expressed as a fraction of a second (e.g., 1/100s). By allowing more light in each frame, a slower shutter speed can cause motion blur in the resulting video if the objects are moving rapidly within the frame. This is particularly relevant for video-based MT systems, which rely on the visual clarity of body landmarks being consistently detectable in each frame. Motion blur reduces the sharpness of these features, making it more difficult for pose estimation algorithms (e.g., MediaPipe, OpenPose, or DeepLabCut) to correctly track landmarks over time. As a result, lower shutter speeds can lead to missed detections, decreased confidence scores, and greater frame-to-frame jitter in landmark trajectories. To empirically demonstrate these effects, we recorded two videos from three synchronized webcams of the same fast-moving gesture (a side-to-side hand-waving motion) at 1/60s (slow) and 1/250s (fast) shutter speeds, as shown in Figure S1, A. We then processed both videos using Mediapipe Holistic to extract the frame-by-frame 3D landmarks for the moving (right) hand and the stationary (left) hand (21 landmarks each). For each camera viewpoint, we quantified 2 key motion tracking metrics: (i) motion jitter - calculated from the frame-to-frame second derivative of the wrist landmark’s 3D trajectory - and (ii) hand visibility - defined as the proportion of frames in which any hand landmarks were detected. Compared to the default 1/60s setting, the faster shutter speed (1/250s) led to substantial improvements in tracking of the moving hand, as visible in substantial reduction in motion jitter (Figure S1, B) and marked improvements in hand visibility (Figure S1, C)
Figure S1. Effects of Shutter Speed on Video-Based Motion Tracking Accuracy. (A) Example frames from the three synchronized webcam views during the fast hand gesture (right hand moving laterally, left hand stationary). Red markers indicate body, hand, and face landmarks extracted by MediaPipe Holistic. (B) Motion jitter values by camera (left) and by hand (right), computed as the frame-to-frame second derivative of the wrist landmark’s 3D position. Faster shutter speed (1/250s) significantly reduced jitter for the moving hand. (C) Hand visibility by camera and hand (left), and percentage improvement in visibility for the faster shutter speed (right). Visibility was defined as the proportion of frames in which any hand landmarks were detected. Faster shutter speed (1/250s) improved tracking robustness for the moving hand across all views, with gains up to +10.7%.
[ Quarto only: see here for more information on the camera and computer equipment ] Each trio of cameras was fed to a Windows PC equipped with a multi-core processor (e.g., Intel i7 or equivalent) capable of encoding and processing the three video streams in parallel. To prevent bandwidth overload and reduce the risk of dropped frames, two of camera-to-PC connections were mediated by a powered USB hub and distributed across separate USB buses wherever possible (e.g., by allocating one camera to a USB 3.0 port and the remaining cameras to separate USB 2.0 controllers). Alternatively, one may use longer Active Optical Cables (AOC) that ensure reliable data transfer over extended distances while maintaining full USB bandwidth, however, this approach still requires the PC to have sufficient separate controller boards to accommodate each camera independently.


1.1.3 Video Recording Procedures
Before recordings, each camera setting was manually configured through the Elgato Camera Hub software to ensure optimal conditions for MT. Specifically, we set the shutter speed to 1/200s to reduce motion blur, downsampled the image resolution to qHD (960 × 540) to minimize data storage demands, and fixed the ISO at 354 to stabilize image brightness and contrast under short exposure times.
[Quarto: here can be screenshot from Elgato Hub] Figure S2. The Elgato Hub Interface
[Quarto Link with Script and Explanation. MML_Video3Cameras_LSL.py] [SCRIPT: 1_LAB_SETUP/VIDEO/MML_Video3Cameras_LSL.py]
We use a custom Python script to record each trio of cameras as a single side-by-side composite video (i.e., concatenating the three feeds horizontally into one file) on two separate computers. This design choice reduces data management overhead compared to handling three separate video files per participant per session. This script leverages the OpenCV (Bradski 2000) and FFmpegCV (Chen, 2022) libraries to feed the combined side-by-side videos from the three cameras into a single compositive video using multithreading, which ensured that all frames were synchronized for each sampling timepoint. To facilitate future processing and debugging, a running frame counter is overlaid on the top-right corner of each of the three concatenated camera views. The video is recorded at 60 Hz in an uncompressed format to preserve image fidelity during acquisition. The script also simultaneously handles LSL integration to allow for post-hoc synchronization of the videos with the other data streams (see Section 1.4.3).
After each session, the raw videos were compressed using the XVID codec at a 2.5x reduction ratio to ease data transfer and storage space using another custom made Python script.
[Quarto Link with Compression Script and Explanation. MML_compression.py] [SCRIPT: 1_LAB_SETUP/VIDEO/MML_Video3Cameras_LSL.py]
1.1.4 - Camera Calibration Procedures: To ensure 3D pose estimation from multi-angle recordings, video-based MT algorithms require prior information on the intrinsic parameters (e.g., focal length, distortion coefficients) and extrinsic parameters (i.e., spatial orientation and position relative to other cameras) of each device (for more information, see Karashchuk et al. 2021). Therefore, before each recording, we performed a calibration procedure for each trio of cameras assigned to a participant. Specifically, we recorded a short (∼1-minute) calibration video using a ChArUco board calibration board (see Figure S2) that was moved systematically throughout the full vertical and horizontal space later occupied by the participant during the experiment. These calibration videos were then used to compute the geometric parameters for 3D triangulation during MT (see ?@sec-process-mt-mt).
Figure S1. Example of Calibration Videos using the ChArUco

1.2 Audio

1.2.1 Choosing the Audio Recording Setup
To obtain a good level of acoustic fidelity, in our MMLab we opted for a high-quality, head-mounted condenser microphone recording independently from the cameras. The reason why we use separate microphones instead of the built-in camera microphone is that the audio quality of these microphones is typically insufficient for high-resolution analyses of speech features such as pitch, intensity and prosody (Švec and Granqvist 2010). Additionally, to stream the audio signal to the LSL, we opted for a Linux-based PC over Windows or macOS because it enables real-time streaming of low-latency, high precision audio thanks to its Advanced Linux Sound Architecture (ALSA).


1.2.2 Audio Recording Equipment
For the microphone, we employed a professional-grade, head-mounted condenser microphone (model: AKG C520, price ~€250) for each participant, as shown in Figure 1C. The head-mounted configuration was important for maintaining a fixed distance between the participant’s mouth and the microphone capsule (essential for measurement of speech amplitude and prosodic features), whilst the cardioid polar pattern further focused sensitivity toward the speaker’s mouth and rejected off-axis environmental noise. Additionally, its built-in shock-mount system helped reduce the mechanical noise generated by body movements. Both microphones were powered via a XLR connection to a DAP PRE-202 low-noise, 2-channel digital amplifier (price: ~€90), which provided a +48V phantom power and included a low-cut filter to suppress low-frequency ambient noise. Input gain on the amplifier was manually fixed at 25% across all recordings to standardize signal levels. From the amplifier, the signal from each microphone was routed via two XLR-to-USB interfaces to two MINIX NEO z83-4 MAX Linux-based mini-PC (price: ~€170).


1.2.3 Audio Recording Procedures
To record and stream the audio to the LSL, we used a custom-made Python script developed in collaboration with Technical Support Group (TSG) at the Donders Institute.
[Quarto Link with Mic Script and Explanation. MML_Microphone.py] [SCRIPT: 1_LAB_SETUP/AUDIO/MML_AudioLSL_Linux_Alsa.py]
The script was executed on each MINIX Linux device and utilized the alsaaudio library to record each signal in mono at a sampling rate of 16 kHz, with 16-bit little-endian encoding optimized for low-latency buffering. This data is directly streamed to the LSL software for multimodal integration and synchronization (see Section 1.4.3). Additionally, to ensure data quality before acquisition and monitor issues such as noise artifacts, clipping, or dropouts, we used a secondary Python script that allowed for real-time graphic visualization of the incoming audio stream.
[Quarto Link with Audio Plot Script and Explanation. MML_Mic_Ploting.py] [SCRIPT: 1_LAB_SETUP/AUDIO/MML_Mic_Plotting.py]
This script pulled the audio stream from LSL and plotted it on a live display that was continuously updated, enabling it to verify waveform quality and monitor for issues such as noise artifacts, clipping, or dropouts.

1.3 Physiology (ECG, EMG, RESP)

1.3.1 Choosing the Physiological Setup
In addition to the video and audio modalities, our MMLab default setup also includes wireless physiological recordings. We selected three modalities that are among the most commonly used in multimodal behavioral research and that are particularly relevant to our proof-of-concept paradigm: electrocardiography (ECG), to capture heart rate dynamics and cardiac synchrony between participants, respiration sensor to measure respiratory activity at the thorax, which is closely tied to vocal production and therefore especially pertinent in a singing task, and surface electromyography (EMG) from the biceps and triceps, to record muscle activation patterns during co-singing gestures. Among all the available proprietary options, we chose the “Biosignals PLUX” recording system for the following reasons: (i) it supports a modular sensor architecture, allowing researchers to buy only the biosensors relevant to their experimental goal; (ii) it transmits all the signals wirelessly (BT), thus granting participants free movement during recordings; (iii) it can be easily integrated with the LSL system, which simplifies synchronization with the other measurements and, finally, it offers a (iv) strong price/quality balance.


1.3.2 Physiological Recording Equipment
As shown in Figure 1C, the equipment consisted of two (one per participant) “biosignalplux Hub” (price: ~€2000, link), each supporting up to 4 input channels and capable of sampling at rates of up to 3000 Hz per channel with 16-bit resolution (Note that an 8-channel biosignalplux Hub is also available, costing ~€4000, link). These devices transmitted data wirelessly via bluetooth in real time to their respective recording computers (the same used for video recordings) using a dedicated bluetooth dongle.
To record participants’ muscle activity, we used two surface EMG sensors per participant (price ~€170, link), one placed over the biceps brachii and one over the triceps brachii of the right arm, allowing us to monitor the activation patterns of both flexor and extensor muscle groups.
As shown in Figure S3, the electrodes were positioned in a bipolar configuration and aligned with the longitudinal axis of each target muscle. The EMG sensors operated in a bipolar differential configuration using two adhesive electrodes (positive and negative). A separate reference (ground) electrode was placed on the participant’s olecranon of the right elbow bone with minimal muscle activity to reduce baseline noise. Prior to electrode placement, the skin was cleaned with an alcohol-based wipe and prepared using abrasive conductive gel (Nuprep) to reduce impedance and enhance signal quality. (documentation). [Quarto: diagram of EMG sensor placement]
Figure S3. EMG electrode placement. Placement at the (A) biceps brachii and (B) triceps brachii. Positive electrode denoted by red, negative denoted by black. Reference electrode was placed on the olecranon of the right elbow (A, top). Figure adapted from BiosignalsPLUX EMG Manual
For cardiac activity, we used the Biosignalplux ECG sensor (price: 140, link) configured for single-lead acquisition in the Einthoven triangle configuration (see Figure S4) (documentation)
[Quarto: diagram of ECG sensor placement]
Figure S4. Electrode placement for single-lead ECG. The positive (red), negative (black) and reference (white) electrodes sit together on the chest because of the short cables (1.5 cm for + and −, 3 cm for reference). They stand in for the Einthoven Lead I positions: left arm (+), right arm (−) and left foot (reference). Figure adapted from BiosignalsPLUX ECG Manual
To record respiratory patterns, we used a piezoelectric respiration sensor (PZT; price ~€140, link) per participant, which allows to record thoracic expansion and contraction during inhalation and exhalation. This was secured around the upper thorax using an adjustable elastic strap (See Figure S5) (documentation)
[Quarto: diagram of Resp belt placement]

1.3.3 Physiological Recording Procedures
Signal acquisition was managed using the OpenSignals (r)evolution software from Biosignalsplux. Using the GUI of the software, we configured the EMGs, ECG and PZT channels to sample at 1000 Hz and visualized these signals in real time to verify signal-to-noise ratio and appropriate signal amplitude across EMG, ECG and respiration channels. These streams are broadcasted to LSL directly via the software (see Section 1.4.3).

1.4 Integration via LabStreamingLayer

1.4.1 Choosing the Integration Setup
A major challenge in multimodal research relates to synchronization and integration of different recordings that operate on distinct hardware platforms, communicate via different software interfaces, rely on independent systems clocks, and sample at different frequencies (Vieira and Cunha 2026). Traditionally, synchronization of multimodal streams has been done post-recording by aligning common timestamped markers acquired during recordings for each modality. However, this approach relies on multiple independent recording computers with device-specific scripts for sending and receiving markers, resulting in decentralized data storage across systems. All of this increases the technical overhead as well as the manual effort during post-alignment. Additionally, even minor issues like latency differences or hardware incompatibilities can introduce significant lags that can easily mis-align the time series, often without any knowledge from the experimenters. For instance, video recordings are prone to dropped frames during acquisition, which, unless properly accounted for by timestamping each frame, can result in de-synchronization that is difficult to detect and correct post hoc.
To address these issues, in our MMLab we decided to implement the LabStreamingLayer (LSL, Kothe et al. 2025), an open-sourced, cross-platform middleware system designed to enable real-time, sub-millisecond synchronization of heterogeneous data streams recorded from different devices. Unlike marker-based synchronization, the LSL creates a shared time base across all incoming data streams using each device’s local monotonic clock. This allows for all the streams to be synchronized at the time of recording and stored in a centralized data format. In addition, LSL is free-to-use, open-source, portable and highly modular, supporting a wide range of recording devices either through native compatibility (like the Biosignalsplux device) or via custom-built LSL “outlet” scripts that stream data into the shared time framework (like our video and audio recording scripts).
[Quarto-only section for LSL Assembly]


1.4.2 LSL Equipment and Assembly
At a system level, the LSL consists of the core liblsl library (Stenner et al. 2022) - a cross-platform API running working on Windows, macOS, and Linux - and associated GUI applications such as the LabRecorder (Kothe et al. 2025). The LSL is built on a simple architecture of Outlets and Inlets. Each recording device broadcasts its stream (i.e., Outlet) via built-in system or via custom-made scripts in the form of descriptive metadata (e.g., stream name, content, type, number of channels, etc.). The receiving application (i.e., Inlet; such as LabRecorder) automatically detects these streams and records them in real time. To achieve multimodal synchronization, the LSL leverages each machine’s local monotonic clock and continuously performs clock offset estimation between the Outlet and Inlet through periodic pinging, which are then used to create a shared time based across all streams with sub-millisecond alignment. This software architecture must be physically implemented through a local network that can span multiple PC’s.
As shown in Figure 1B–C, our setup comprised two Windows PCs, each connected to three wired video cameras and wireless physiological sensors, and two Linux mini PCs, each connected to a wired audio stream. A third Windows PC was then used to centrally record all these synchronized data streams using the LSL’s LabRecorder. All machines were interconnected via a wired Gigabit Ethernet local area network (LAN) using a shared 5-port Gigabit switch (model used: NETGEAR GS305v3).


1.4.3 LSL Stream Integration
Each recording script described in Sections ?@sec-exp-design (stimulus presentation) 1.1, (video), 1.2 (audio) and 1.3 (physiology) integrates LSL using either the pylsl Python library (Kothe et al. 2025) or the recording software’s built-in LSL integration (e.g., Opensignals Revolution). For the stimulus presentation, the script sent marker events to the LSL Inlet via user’s button-presses, with pre-defined names to mark the start-end of trials and conditions. For the videos, rather than streaming the raw RGB images (which would be prohibitively large for real-time streaming), the script streams the current frame numbers to LSL (at 500 Hz), which are then used to align the raw video files with other modalities in post-processing. For the audio, the recording script captures sound in small chunks and pushes each chunk to LSL as it is filled. Each chunk contains 160 samples, which, at a 16,000 Hz sampling rate, corresponds to 10 milliseconds of audio. This chunking (rather than sampling) is a practical compromise that keeps the latency low, whilst avoiding pushing data to LSL so frequently that it overloads the system (for more information on LSL timings, see here). For physiology, the streams are broadcasted directly to LSL via OpenSignals’ built-in integration (see documentation) at 1000 Hz, producing three streams (per participant) each containing two raw EMG channels, one ECG, and one PZT signal.


1.4.4 LSL Recording Procedures
Prior to each recording, the LabRecorder allowed us to check the presence of all expected streams from both participants. Once confirmed, recording was initiated through the LabRecorder interface, resulting in a single .xdf file. For audio and physiology, this file contains the full time-series data (with metadata) for both participants. For video, the .xdf file contains only per-frame metadata (timestamp and frame index for each each of the three camera views), while the corresponding raw video files were saved locally on the respective Windows PC and later linked to this metadata during post-processing (see Section X).

Introduction
Human behavior is multimodal and dynamic in nature. From the precise integration of visual, somatosensory and vestibular information when walking (MacKinnon 2018), to the effortless coordination of speech, gestures and facial expressions when communicating (Holler and Levinson 2019), our actions continuously unfold through multiple sensory, haptic and motor signals that interact across time and space. Yet, researchers investigating different aspects of human behavior in the context of psychological and neurocognitive sciences have traditionally relied on temporally coarse-grained, unimodal measures: e.g., capturing only one type of signal at a time, often through indirect proxies such as self-report questionnaires (Baumeister, Vohs, and Funder 2007), button presses, or accuracy scores (Maselli et al. 2023; Parsons, Kruijt, and Fox 2019).
In recent years, however, the research landscape in cognitive science has changed dramatically. Technological and methodological advancements in sensing equipment, recording devices and computational tools that handle high-dimensional data have paved the way for a new era of behavioral research, moving several interdisciplinary fields from unimodal to multimodal approaches Yang (2019). In the last decade alone, more than sixty thousand scientific publications within social sciences have appeared with the term “multimodal” in their keywords, marking a 400% increase from the previous decade (based on a Scopus keyword search conducted in 2025).
In contrast to the past, where measurements were limited to either unimodal proxies or laborious manual labelling of observed behaviors (e.g., Brugman and Russel 2004), nowadays researchers can employ high-frequency sensing devices to simultaneously capture movements, speech, physiological changes, gaze patterns, and even neural activity, as they unfold in real time. For instance, optical motion tracking systems such as OptiTrack (Nagymáté and Kiss 2018) can be combined with wearable eye trackers (Gunawardena, Ginige, and Javadi 2022) and electrophysiological recordings (Moon and Lee 2023) to study complex intra- and inter-personal brain-behavior dynamics of phenomena such as neural synchrony (e.g., Koul et al. 2023), cognitive workload (e.g., Charles and Nixon 2019) or psychosocial stress (e.g., Richer et al. 2024). Accordingly, the progress in technological infrastructures has enabled a similar progress in the level of spatio-temporal granularity with which researchers can ask and answer questions about different neuro-cognitive-behavioral phenomena (Laudańska et al. 2025).
Despite these technological advancements, there are important methodological challenges that will shape the future directions of this emerging field. To start, building a functioning multimodal laboratory from scratch can be both technically complex and prohibitively costly for many researchers. Firstly, one needs to select the appropriate recording system for each modality, a choice that can be particularly overwhelming given the sheer number of different manufacturers, pricing ranges and technical specifications. For instance, there are currently dozens of commercially available motion tracking (MT) systems, spanning a wide range of technologies – from high-precision optical systems (e.g., Vicon, Qualisys, Optitrack) to wearable inertial sensors (e.g., Xsen, Noraxon), to markerless computer vision tools (e.g., OpenPose, MediaPipe) – and costing from few hundred, to hundreds of thousands euros (for a comprehensive review, see Juveriyah, Himanshu, and Moharkan 2023).
Secondly, assembling all multiple recording devices (MT, microphones, physiological sensors, etc.) in a spatially efficient and modular setup without interfering with participants’ natural behaviors presents design and logistical challenges. For instance, many commercially available setups are only tailored to fixed laboratory environments, rely on heavy infrastructure, and are primarily designed for single-participant recordings, making them difficult to relocate or adapt the laboratory to real-world settings and/or multiple participants (Ladouce et al. 2017; Maselli et al. 2023).
Thirdly, a major challenge lies in integrating and synchronizing the heterogeneous data streams that all of these recording devices produce. In fact, each modality (whether MT, audio, gaze or physiology) is sampled at different rates (e.g., ranging from 60 Hz for videos to 16 kHz for audio), recorded using different hardware and software, and encoded in different formats (Vieira and Cunha 2026). Ensuring that all these signals are temporally aligned with sufficient precision and stored in an integrated and accessible format is non-trivial, especially in studies involving many recording devices in highly naturalistic paradigms with multiple interacting participants.
Finally, even after data collection, researchers are faced with the substantial demands of managing and analyzing multi-dimensional, time-varying datasets (such as dozens of 2D video streams, high-resolution audio, and continuous physiological signals) all of which need to be pre-processed, and organized for analysis. Without standardized pipelines or centralized data structures, this process can become fragmented and error-prone, especially when integrating data from multiple participants or sessions.
In most cases, researchers have outsourced these challenges to proprietary companies that manufacture recording systems with accompanied blackboxed software, with further help from technical support staff in the case of high-resourced institutions. To capture participants movements, one might indeed conveniently opt for a state-of-the-art MT system from a proprietary company that usually offers extensive customer support (including installation), optimal recording accuracy, and a user-friendly software with built-in analyses packages (Merriaux et al. 2017; van der Kruk and Reijne 2018). While these proprietary solutions offer clear advantages, they also come with some important drawbacks: they are often prohibitively expensive (e.g., Qualisys: circa 150-200K €, Vicon: 200-250K €), relying on closed-sourced software and analyses toolkits, often with monthly subscription costs (van Schaik and Dominici 2020). As a result, they are not accessible to many researchers or institutions working with limited budgets (e.g., in low-middle income countries), nor easily adaptable for use in non-standard experimental setups or in field-based research. Additionally, even when the budget allows, the issue of data integration and synchronization across different devices (e.g., an MT system with physiological sensors) still remains, as each proprietary device (typically) operates within closed device/software ecosystems that can make cross-platform integration challenging at many levels.
Given this context, a central question within the field of multimodal research is: how much should we rely on these proprietary systems, and how much should we instead invest in building intellectual capital toward more affordable, open-source alternatives? Beyond the drawbacks outlined above, an exclusive reliance on proprietary commercial systems can also hinder the sharing of knowledge required to build and operate multimodal setups, which risks being locked behind licenses, paywalled documentation, or the institutional memory of well-funded labs. Therefore, we believe that investing in alternatives can help democratize access to multimodal research and foster a more equitable and collaborative scientific ecosystem, where researchers engage in open pedagogical practices and actively contribute to the development, adaptation, and dissemination of methodological tools (Woelfle, Olliaro, and Todd 2011).
With this in mind, here we introduce the Mobile Multimodal Laboratory (MMLab). The MMLab project provides an affordable, open-source solution to anyone interested in capturing multimodal human behaviors in both controlled and ecological environments. It comprises a suite of freely available resources – i.e., the present paper, a detailed Quarto manual and a comprehensive coding repository – specifically designed to guide users through all the steps entailed in building a fully functional mobile multimodal lab, including synchronizing, recording, and analysing data streams of interest. The MMLab was built around the following key features:


Accessibility: all documentation, code, and tutorials are open sourced to ensure broad accessibility, transparency, and reuse across research communities.
Affordability: the proposed setup (video recording optimized for 3D motion tracking, audio-recording, and physiological signals from two participants) can be fully assembled for under 10,000€, as it relies on low-cost components and, whenever possible, non-proprietary hardware and software.
Portability: MMLab is designed to be compact and easily transportable, allowing researchers to use it in a range of testing environments beyond traditional lab spaces.
Built-in Integration and Synchronization: data from each recording device is centrally integrated through the LabStreamingLayer (LSL, Kothe et al. 2025), which allows for precise temporal synchronization of multimodal streams at the level of recording.
Modularity: the setup supports a wide range of interchangeable components and sensors compatible with LSL, allowing researchers to customize the lab to suit specific research goals.
Community-maintenance: MMLab aims to gather researchers interested in expanding and maintaining the current infrastructure to ensure longevity of the project, solve common troubleshooting issues, or implement demands from the community.

AnalysisOverview Code

1.1 Signal Normalization
Because these signals originate from different modalities with different physical units and amplitude ranges (e.g., volts for ECG, metres for motion, normalized amplitude for audio), each signal was first z-scored (mean subtracted and divided by the standard deviation), placing it on a common numerical scale so that the subsequent density estimation is not biased by differences in raw units or amplitude ranges.
[CODE: 4b_SynchronyAnalyses/MML_Mutual_Information_Analyses.ipynb#mi-zscore]

1.2 Mutual Information (MI) Analyses
To quantify the statistical dependency between the two participants’ continuous signals we used MI, a measure grounded in information theory and closely related to Shannon entropy (Shannon 1948). MI captures how much knowing the value of one signal reduces the uncertainty about the other in both linear and non-linear dependencies, expressed in a non-negative scale where 0 indicates no statistical dependency and higher values indicating stronger coupling (with no upper-bound)
Computing MI requires estimating how likely each signal is to take certain values (its marginal density), and how likely two signals are to take specific combinations of values at the same time point (their joint density). Because our signals are continuous-valued, these densities cannot be obtained by counting occurrences (as one would do with discrete signals) and must instead be estimated. Therefore, we used Gaussian Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) from scipy package to capture smooth probability density functions as estimates of these densities (Silverman 1986). KDE works by centering a small Gaussian curve on every individual data point and aggregating them, resulting in a series of curves that accumulate into high-density peaks where data points overlap frequently or low peaks in regions where data is sparse.The width of each Gaussian kernel was determined automatically based on the spread of the data (using automatic bandwidth selection). This procedure was applied three times per signal pair: once for each of the two signals individually (yielding the marginal densities) and once for the two participants’ corresponding signals jointly in two-dimensional space (yielding the joint density).
[CODE: 4b_SynchronyAnalyses/MML_Mutual_Information_Analyses.ipynb#mi-kde]
MI was then computed by comparing the joint density against the product of the two marginal densities. Under statistical independence, the joint density would equal the product of the marginals exactly (i.e., knowing one signal would give no information about the other). MI quantifies the departure from this independence assumption by evaluating the log-ratio of the joint density to the product of the marginals, weighting each log-ratio by the joint density, and integrating numerically over the full density surface. The resulting value is expressed in nats (natural logarithm units) and is always non-negative.
[CODE: 4b_SynchronyAnalyses/MML_Mutual_Information_Analyses.ipynb#mi-compute]
To ensure that the MI estimate captured dependencies even when one signal slightly leads or trails the other, MI was computed at seven time lags (−300, −200, −100, 0, +100, +200, and +300 ms) per signal pair. After each lag-based subsetting, both signals were smoothed with a Savitzky–Golay filter (window = 100 ms, polynomial order = 2) to reduce residual sampling jitter. The maximum MI value across all lags was retained as the summary coupling statistic for each pair.
[CODE: 4b_SynchronyAnalyses/MML_Mutual_Information_Analyses.ipynb#mi-lag-smooth]
This analysis was applied in a sliding-window fashion across each trial, using 5-second windows advancing in 1-second steps, yielding a time-resolved estimate of coupling strength. Windows containing fewer than 100 time points, or fewer than 50 valid (non-NaN) samples for either variable, were excluded.
[CODE: 4b_SynchronyAnalyses/MML_Mutual_Information_Analyses.ipynb#mi-window]
MI was computed for all 64 between-participant signal pairs (8 signals: right_index x-y-z, audio, respiration, ECG, EMG_bicep, EMG_tricep; for P1 and P2) covering both within-modality coupling (e.g., Audio P1 - Audio P2) and cross-modality coupling (e.g., Audio P1 - ECG P2). Though within-participant pairs were computed, the analysis focuses exclusively on interpersonal coupling. Each window’s result was stored with its condition labels (Vision/NoVision × Movement/NoMovement), trial identifier, window index, and the pair classification.






Figure 1: NEED THE PROPER FIGURE Two interacting participants are shown (P: left; P2: right) each with their recorded signals: motion tracking (camera, blue) audio (microphone, red), ECG (heart, purple), respiration (lungs, purple) and EMG (bicep and tricep, purple). Each full circle represents the entropy of one signal: H(X) for P1 and H(Y) for P2. The overlap, I(X;Y), is the mutual information, i.e., how much knowing one reduces uncertainty about the other. The non-overlapping parts of each circle, H(X|Y) and H(Y|X), are the uncertainty that remains in each signal once the other is known. The total area covered by both circles is the joint entropy, H(X,Y).

title: Mobile Multimodal Lab
text:
MobileMultimodalLab (MMLab) is a project initiated by researchers at Donders Center for Cognition. It aims to provide a lab setup for anyone interested in studying multimodal interactive behaviour - including acoustics, body movement, muscle activity, eye movements, and so on.
To achieve this, we are working on a comprehensive coding library, accompanied by a practical manual, that shall help researchers to build their own MobileMultimodalLab. Our guiding principles are:

Open-source resources - All code and documentation is freely available to everyone
Low-cost equipment - We want to build the setup with as little monetary cost as possible (i.e., less than 10K)
Portable setup - The setup should be easily transportable across locations




MobileMultimodalLab


The MML setup originally consists of

multiple frame-synced 2D cameras that allow for 3D motion tracking
multiple microphones for acoustic analysis
multiple physiological sensors for measuring heart rate, muscle activity, and respiration

To ensure that all the signals are synchronized, we use the Lab streaming layer (https://github.com/sccn/labstreaminglayer), a software that synchronizes different data streams with sub-millisecond precision, crucially simplifying the data collection process and subsequent processing.



Setup


Additionally, the setup is build in a modular way, so that anyone can add or remove equipment and recording from the default setup as long as these devices are LSL compatible

title: Load necessary libraries
text:
First, we are importing libraries (also known as “packages”) that we will use throughout this notebook. In this case, we are using pathlib, numpy, and plotly. If they are not installed, we will install them.
Pathlib provides methods to handle file and directory paths, numpy allows us to handle arrays, and plotly is the graphing library we will use for visualization.
If any of these libraries are not installed, we install them directly from this notebook.

title: Load necessary libraries
text:
1 Define variables
Next, we’re defining a few things we’ll need to use later:

path_to_recording: This is a path to the folder where the mocap data for this recording is stored
joint_to_plot: We need to tell the program which joint we want to visualize. By default, we select the ‘nose’.
mediapipe_indices: These are the possible joints that can be visualized.

You can select a different joint from mediapipe_indices to view the plot for that - for example, you could replace joint_to_plot = 'nose' with joint_to_plot = 'left_elbow' to view the trajectory visualization for the left elbow.
We’re also getting the path to two types of data we need - ‘center of mass’ and ‘3D body data’. We will be loading and using these datasets later on.

title: Load necessary libraries
text:
2 Plotting
After loading our data, we are going to create some plots to better visualize it. Specifically, we are plotting the trajectory of the total body center of mass and the trajectory of the chosen joint (nose by default, but you can replace that and rerun this notebook to plot a different trajectory).
The first three plots (in column 1) represent the X, Y, and Z trajectories of the total body center of mass. The next three plots (in column 2) represent the X, Y, and Z trajectories of the chosen joint.
Note: The X, Y, and Z values refer to the three dimensions in space.
You can click and drag on the plots below to interact with them and zoom into certain areas. When hovering over the plot, you can see additional options in the top right to pan, zoom, reset, and download the plots.

title: Load necessary libraries
text:
3 3D Plotting
Finally, we are creating a 3D plot of the skeleton movement, tracking all the joints in the mediapipe_indices list over time.
The ‘Play’ button at the bottom allows you to watch the motion as if it were a video. Before pressing play, you can manually click and drag the plot around to orient the view of the plot.

title: Load necessary libraries
text:
First, we are importing libraries (also known as “packages”) that we will use throughout this notebook. In this case, we are using pathlib, numpy, and plotly. If they are not installed, we will install them.
Pathlib provides methods to handle file and directory paths, numpy allows us to handle arrays, and plotly is the graphing library we will use for visualization.
If any of these libraries are not installed, we install them directly from this notebook.

title: Load necessary libraries
text:
1 Define variables
Next, we’re defining a few things we’ll need to use later:

path_to_recording: This is a path to the folder where the mocap data for this recording is stored
joint_to_plot: We need to tell the program which joint we want to visualize. By default, we select the ‘nose’.
mediapipe_indices: These are the possible joints that can be visualized.

You can select a different joint from mediapipe_indices to view the plot for that - for example, you could replace joint_to_plot = 'nose' with joint_to_plot = 'left_elbow' to view the trajectory visualization for the left elbow.
We’re also getting the path to two types of data we need - ‘center of mass’ and ‘3D body data’. We will be loading and using these datasets later on.

title: Load necessary libraries
text:
2 Plotting
After loading our data, we are going to create some plots to better visualize it. Specifically, we are plotting the trajectory of the total body center of mass and the trajectory of the chosen joint (nose by default, but you can replace that and rerun this notebook to plot a different trajectory).
The first three plots (in column 1) represent the X, Y, and Z trajectories of the total body center of mass. The next three plots (in column 2) represent the X, Y, and Z trajectories of the chosen joint.
Note: The X, Y, and Z values refer to the three dimensions in space.
You can click and drag on the plots below to interact with them and zoom into certain areas. When hovering over the plot, you can see additional options in the top right to pan, zoom, reset, and download the plots.

title: Load necessary libraries
text:
3 3D Plotting
Finally, we are creating a 3D plot of the skeleton movement, tracking all the joints in the mediapipe_indices list over time.
The ‘Play’ button at the bottom allows you to watch the motion as if it were a video. Before pressing play, you can manually click and drag the plot around to orient the view of the plot.

## Requirements Please install the necessary packages in requirements. ## OVERVIEWE This Python script splits single videos containing multiple cameras views into individual videos of each separate view using OpenCV. It outputs the split video files into a specific folder structure, making them ready for further processing, such as motion tracking with tools like OpenPose or Pose2Sim. Below is an overview of the key steps in the code:

Importing Necessary Packages: see requirements.txt for all necessary packages
Defining Relevant Directories, Variables, and Functions: Working with relative paths, the scripts defines input and output folders. Video extension (e.g., *.avi) and corresponding codec extension (e.g., XVID) can be ajusted by the user accordingly. The current script assumes 3 cameras for each vidoe, each of them with an euqal height and width. The split_camera_views function is defined to handle the core task of splitting a video file into separate camera views. This function processes each video file, extracting frames and dividing them into distinct sections corresponding to different camera views. The split videos are then saved to specified output files.
and 2a. In 2 the script automatically scans a specified directory to identify and collect all video files with a specific extension (e.g., .avi). This allows for batch processing of multiple videos without requiring manual file selection. In 2a, the the script provides an option for the user to manually select one or more video files through a graphical file dialog. This feature offers flexibility for the user to choose specific videos from any directory for processing.
The scripts loops through the selected or identified video files and splitting each one into separate camera views: For each video file, the script extracts the filename and generates output file paths for each camera view (e.g., _cam1.avi, _cam2.avi, _cam3.avi). The split_camera_views function is called to process the video, splitting it into three separate camera views and saving them in a structured folder, such as a raw-2d subfolder within the output directory.

title: Load necessary libraries
text:
First, we are importing libraries (also known as “packages”) that we will use throughout this notebook. In this case, we are using pathlib, numpy, and plotly. If they are not installed, we will install them.
Pathlib provides methods to handle file and directory paths, numpy allows us to handle arrays, and plotly is the graphing library we will use for visualization.
If any of these libraries are not installed, we install them directly from this notebook.

title: Load necessary libraries
text:
1 Define variables
Next, we’re defining a few things we’ll need to use later:

path_to_recording: This is a path to the folder where the mocap data for this recording is stored
joint_to_plot: We need to tell the program which joint we want to visualize. By default, we select the ‘nose’.
mediapipe_indices: These are the possible joints that can be visualized.

You can select a different joint from mediapipe_indices to view the plot for that - for example, you could replace joint_to_plot = 'nose' with joint_to_plot = 'left_elbow' to view the trajectory visualization for the left elbow.
We’re also getting the path to two types of data we need - ‘center of mass’ and ‘3D body data’. We will be loading and using these datasets later on.

title: Load necessary libraries
text:
2 Plotting
After loading our data, we are going to create some plots to better visualize it. Specifically, we are plotting the trajectory of the total body center of mass and the trajectory of the chosen joint (nose by default, but you can replace that and rerun this notebook to plot a different trajectory).
The first three plots (in column 1) represent the X, Y, and Z trajectories of the total body center of mass. The next three plots (in column 2) represent the X, Y, and Z trajectories of the chosen joint.
Note: The X, Y, and Z values refer to the three dimensions in space.
You can click and drag on the plots below to interact with them and zoom into certain areas. When hovering over the plot, you can see additional options in the top right to pan, zoom, reset, and download the plots.

title: Load necessary libraries
text:
3 3D Plotting
Finally, we are creating a 3D plot of the skeleton movement, tracking all the joints in the mediapipe_indices list over time.
The ‘Play’ button at the bottom allows you to watch the motion as if it were a video. Before pressing play, you can manually click and drag the plot around to orient the view of the plot.

Next, we’re defining a few things we’ll need to use later:

path_to_recording: This is a path to the folder where the mocap data for this recording is stored
joint_to_plot: We need to tell the program which joint we want to visualize. By default, we select the ‘nose’.
mediapipe_indices: These are the possible joints that can be visualized.

You can select a different joint from mediapipe_indices to view the plot for that - for example, you could replace joint_to_plot = 'nose' with joint_to_plot = 'left_elbow' to view the trajectory visualization for the left elbow.
We’re also getting the path to two types of data we need - ‘center of mass’ and ‘3D body data’. We will be loading and using these datasets later on.

title: Load necessary libraries
text:
2 Plotting
After loading our data, we are going to create some plots to better visualize it. Specifically, we are plotting the trajectory of the total body center of mass and the trajectory of the chosen joint (nose by default, but you can replace that and rerun this notebook to plot a different trajectory).
The first three plots (in column 1) represent the X, Y, and Z trajectories of the total body center of mass. The next three plots (in column 2) represent the X, Y, and Z trajectories of the chosen joint.
Note: The X, Y, and Z values refer to the three dimensions in space.
You can click and drag on the plots below to interact with them and zoom into certain areas. When hovering over the plot, you can see additional options in the top right to pan, zoom, reset, and download the plots.

title: Load necessary libraries
text:
3 3D Plotting
Finally, we are creating a 3D plot of the skeleton movement, tracking all the joints in the mediapipe_indices list over time.
The ‘Play’ button at the bottom allows you to watch the motion as if it were a video. Before pressing play, you can manually click and drag the plot around to orient the view of the plot.

1 Discussion
The MMLab was developed to provide an accessible, low-cost, and open-source solution for capturing multimodal human behaviors in both lab-based and ecological environments. Rather than a single piece of software or hardware, the MMLab is a suite of freely available resources – comprising the present paper, an extended Quarto book, and an accompanying GitHub repository. Together, they function as an end-to-end blueprint for assembling a multimodal recording system, executing recording procedures, and processing and analyzing the resulting data streams.
The tutorial-style structure of this manuscript walks the reader through each step of this pipeline. Grounding all procedures in our proof-of-concept experiment (?@sec-exp, a structured interpersonal singing task with a 2×2 (Vision × Movement) design), ?@sec-setup described the setup of the MMLab, covering the choice and configuration of hardware for video, audio, wireless physiology (ECG, EMG, respiration), and the central integration of all streams through the LSL. ?@sec-preproc dealt with multimodal wrangling and stream preprocessing, describing signal extraction from the unitary file, stream segmentation and multimodal re-merging. ?@sec-process covered multimodal signal processing, including full 3D motion-tracking pipeline, extraction of audio amplitude envelopes, heart rate, muscle activation, and respiratory waveforms, ending with the merging of all filtered signals onto a multimodal array. Finally, ?@sec-analysis presents a proof-of-concept analysis using mutual information, quantifying interpersonal coupling across vocal, physiological, and kinematic channels between the two co-singing participants.
Across these sections, the MMLab was consistently built around five complementary principles. First, in terms of accessibility, all documentation, code, and tutorials are fully open-sourced. The intent is not only to make the tools available, but to make the technical knowledge behind them transparent and reusable. This lowers the barrier to entry for new users and serves as a pedagogical resource for students and technical staff, as well as offering the opportunity for others to contribute and improve on our designs. Second, in terms of affordability, we demonstrated that a lab capable of simultaneously capturing video (for 3D motion tracking), high-fidelity audio, and wireless physiological signals from two interacting participants can be fully assembled for under €10,000 using off-the shelf consumer-grade components and open-source software Third, in terms of portability, the MMLab allows for mobile research: the recording equipment and laptops can be transported inside simple suitcases and reassembled outside of a fixed laboratory room. This opens the door to field-based, ecologically valid recordings that are typically inaccessible to heavy, room-mounted commercial setups. Fourth, in terms of integration and synchronization, the LabStreamingLayer (LSL) serves as the unifying backbone of the MMLab, solving one of the most persistent bottlenecks in multimodal research (i.e., sub-millisecond synchronization of heterogeneous data streams recorded on different machines, operating systems, and sampling rates) without requiring proprietary middleware. Fifth, in terms of modularity, MMLab is intended to beMMLab is intended to be easily extensible beyond the specific configuration described here. Any device with a native LSL outlet (or a simple python wrapper, as we demonstrated for video and audio) can be added to the pipeline, leaving any user (or future developments of MMLab) with opportunities to add or substitute any modality, leaving any user (or future developments of MMLab) with opportunities to add or substitute any modality (e.g., eye-tracking, EEG, additional biosensors, VR headsets, or additional participants) without rebuilding the underlying infrastructure.
Beyond these technical contributions, the MMLab is motivated by a broader concern about ecological validity in the study of human behavior. Historically, psychological, cognitive, and neuroscientific research has relied heavily on temporally coarse-grained, unimodal measures: self-reports and Likert-scale questionnaires in social psychology (Baumeister, Vohs, and Funder 2007), button presses and accuracy scores in cognitive and neuropsychological work (Maselli et al. 2023; Parsons, Kruijt, and Fox 2019). This was largely a pragmatic choice: until recently, capturing the temporally rich, multimodal reality of behavior was methodologically prohibitive (Bateman 2016; Sanbonmatsu, Cooley, and Butner 2021). However, although these unimodal measures are valuable for many research questions, they are inherently limited for others. For instance, a Likert-scale rating of how often a person gestures during conversation cannot substitute for a quantitative measure of the movement itself –– its speed, amplitude, or coupling with concurrent speech (Pouw, Trujillo, and Dixon 2020). Gestures during conversation are tightly coupled with speech prosody (add classical refs instead of Pouw et al. 2020), modulated by turn-taking dynamics (Kendrick, Holler, and Levinson 2023), and shaped by mutual visibility (Holler et al. 2014; Mol et al. 2011) in temporally extended and distributed processes shaped by their social context (Pouw et al. 2014; Streeck, Goodwin, and LeBaron 2011; Trujillo and Holler 2023). Similarly, emotional and affective states are increasingly understood as dynamic processes that emerge from the continuous interplay between central nervous system activity, peripheral physiology, and overt bodily behavior (D’Mello and Kory 2015; Mauss and Robinson 2009). Capturing such states therefore requires jointly measuring the neural, autonomic, and behavioral dynamics that co-constitute them, rather than any single channel or proxy in isolation.
In this context, the MMLab is a methodological response to the current and future state of research across these fields. By making the technical infrastructure for synchronized, multi-stream recording available at a fraction of the previous cost, it enables researchers to move from proxies for behavior to direct measurements of behavior and its underlying neural and physiological signals –– and it makes this move available to labs that would otherwise be priced out of such work. Taken together, this matters both for equity of access and for the diversity of research questions that get asked. In this sense, MMLab contributes to a broader movement in which the question is no longer whether behavior can be captured multimodally, but which embodied processes and inter-personal dynamics become tractable objects of scientific inquiry.
Alongside its strengths, the MMLab comes with some important limitations. The most obvious is the absence of the institutional and commercial support that accompanies off-the-shelf systems. When a lab purchases a commercial motion-tracking system, it gains more than hardware: installation, calibration support, warranty replacements, and a vendor to call when something breaks. The MMLab has none of this. It is a collection of documented components held together by open-source software which shifts the burden of maintenance, troubleshooting, and repair onto the developer community and, ultimately, onto the users themselves. A related limitation is that the MMLab presupposes a baseline of technical literacy. Although we have deliberately documented every step in prose and opted for extensive code comments, the pipeline still assumes some familiarity with Python, the command line, basic networking, and the logic of digital signal processing. The tutorial aims to lower this barrier, but it does not eliminate it.
The biggest practical challenge remains the robustness of the multimodal setup. Every component of the MMLab is prone to errors – as in any recording setup, commercial or otherwise. While the setup has been validated in a proof-of-concept experiment and the pipeline is written to prevent common issues and support individual troubleshooting, problems will arise, including in configurations we cannot anticipate, since users will adapt the setup to hardware and environments we have not tested. Here we list the most recurring problems. First, synchronization: LSL’s clock-offset estimation can degrade under heavy WLAN traffic, and consumer-grade devices with irregular sampling rates can even violate the assumptions of LSL’s built-in jitter correction (Kothe et al. 2025). In practice, a wired network and manual inspection of inter-stream offsets after each session are essential. Second, data acquisition: Depending on the data stream being recorded, larger setups face bandwidth constraints. For instance, consumer-grade USB cameras drop frames when bandwidth is saturated, so the pipeline has to be built assuming drops will occur. Third, resource contention: pushing too many high-bandwidth streams through a single node can produce gaps in the recorded data via LabStreamingLayer (Kothe et al. 2025), and streams recorded on the same machine compete for CPU, disk, and bus resources, so a problem in one stream can propagate to others. None of these issues are fatal, but all require careful pre-testing and some iterative debugging.
Finally, the operational limitations above concern whether the system records; a separate question is what it records. The MMLab relies largely on consumer-grade sensors and approximating algorithms. Even a flawlessly executed session will not match the spatial and temporal precision of a commercial marker-based system (consider, for instance, 0.05 mm error for OptiTrack vs. 1.5 cm error for computer-vision motion capture). For many behavioral research questions, however, this ceiling is well above what the analysis requires: the effects of interest in multimodal communication typically live at the scale of gestures, postures, and prosodic contours rather than sub-millimeter displacements, and consumer-grade capture resolves them comfortably. Moreover, the modularity of the MMLab allows precision to be concentrated where a given study needs it: a camera can be positioned for close capture of the face or hands when fine articulatory or manual details is the target, sampling rates and resolutions can be raised for the streams that carry the effect of interest, and less critical modalities can be recorded more coarsely to conserve bandwidth. Rather than delivering uniform high precision at uniform high cost, the MMLab lets researchers allocate fidelity to match their question. The MMLab is thus not a one-click, black-box solution that works automatically in every environment with every device. It is, however, a transparent and extensible one. We intend to continue improving the pipeline, which includes building a community of developers willing to maintain existing functionalities, add new features (e.g. modalities), and document recurring user issues.
Looking forward, we see the MMLab less as a finished product and more as a continuously evolving system that adapts to new technology and contributions from other users. The long-term viability of an open system depends on the community that maintains it. We intend to establish a clear contribution model that lowers the barrier to adding features, fixing bugs, and extending documentation, together with a versioning scheme that lets users track changes and reproduce earlier configurations reliably. Adding features also include implementation of new modalities or data streams. Since MMLab is built on the LabStreamingLayer architecture, any LSL-compatible device can in principle be integrated. Additions such as eye-tracking, electromagnetic articulography (EMA), Electroencephalography (EEG) and others would broaden the range of questions the MMLab can address, particularly those linking overt communicative behavior to underlying physiological states.
Alongside new developments, future efforts shall also focus on lowering the technical barrier. Containerization (e.g. using Docker) could package the software environment so that setup no longer depends on manual installation and dependency management; configuration templates could provide validated starting points for common recording scenarios; a lightweight graphical interface would make stream selection and session control accessible without the command line; and a quality-control dashboard would surface inter-stream offsets, dropped frames, and other diagnostics for inspection immediately after each session. Together, these would move the MMLab closer to usability by researchers without a strong programming background.
Taken together, these developments point toward what we see as the central promise of the MMLab: not simply a cheaper alternative to commercial systems, but a broadening of who can do multimodal research, where, and on whom. Because the setup is portable, it enables recording in contexts outside the lab – naturalistic and field settings, developmental populations such as caregiver-infant dyads, and older or clinical groups for whom travelling to a lab is itself a barrier to participation. Because it is affordable and open, it lowers the threshold for laboratories or individuals without the budget for proprietary systems, and for research communities and regions in which such equipment has simply been out of reach, widening both the range of questions that can be asked and the diversity of populations from which answers are drawn. And because every component, from acquisition to analysis, is documented and inspectable, studies built on the MMLab are reproducible by construction, and the setup itself becomes a shared, extensible foundation that the community can adapt rather than a black box that each lab must trust on faith. Multimodal behavior is among the richest windows onto human behavior. Our hope is that the MMLab helps open that window to a wider range of researchers, settings, and participants than current tools allow.
