title: Mobile Multimodal Lab
text:
In recent years the research landscape in cognitive science has changed dramatically. Technological and methodological advancements in sensing equipment, recording devices and computational tools that handle high-dimensional data have paved the way for a new era of behavioral research, moving several interdisciplinary fields from unimodal to multimodal approaches (e.g., see Turk, 2014; Yang, 2019) for reviews). In the last decade alone, more than 60 thousand scientific publications have appeared with the term “multimodal” in their keywords, marking a 400% increase from the previous decade (source: Scopus, 2025). In contrast to the past, where measurements were limited to either unimodal proxies or laborious manual labelling of observed behaviors (e.g., Brugman & Russel, 2014.), nowadays researchers can employ state-of-the-art motion tracking systems [e.g., “Vicon”, Pfister et al., 2014) or OptiTrack, Nagymáté & Kiss, 2018)] alongside high-frequency sensing devices [e.g., wereable eye trackers, (Gunawardena et al., 2022)or electrophysiological recordings (Moon & Lee, 2023)] to simultaneously capture movements, speech, physiological changes, gaze patterns, and even neural states, as they unfold in real time. For instance, combined electroencephalographic, kinematic and eye-tracking recordings can reveal the intra- and inter-personal brain-behavior dynamics of phenomena such as neural synchrony (e.g., (Koul et al., 2023), cognitive workload (e.g., Charles & Nixon, 2019) or psychosocial stress (e.g., Richer et al., 2024). Accordingly, the progress in technological infrastructures has yielded a similar progress in the level of spatio-temporal granularity with which researchers can ask and answer questions about different neuro-cognitive-behavioral phenomena.
Despite these technological advancements, there are important methodological challenges that will shape the future directions of this emerging field. To start, building a functioning multimodal laboratory from scratch can be both technically complex and prohibitively costly for many researchers. Firstly, one needs to select the appropriate recording system for each modality, a choice that can be particularly overwhelming given the sheer number of different manufactures, pricing ranges and technical specifications. For instance, there are currently dozens of commercially available motion tracking (MT) systems, spanning a wide range of technologies – from high-precision optical systems (e.g., Vicon, Qualisys) to wearable inertial sensors (e.g., Xsen, Noraxon), and from markerless computer vision tools (e.g., OpenPose, MediaPipe) to pressure-based platforms (e.g., AMTI force plates) – and costing from few hundred (e.g., standard USB cameras) to hundreds of thousands euros (e.g., e.g., multi-camera Vicon system). Secondly, assembling all multiple recording devices (MT, microphones, physiological sensors, etc.) in a spatially efficient and modular setup without interfering with participants natural behaviors poses design and logistical challenges. For instance, many commercially available setups are only tailored to fixed laboratory environments, rely on heavy infrastructure, and are primarily designed for single-participant recordings, making them difficult to relocate or adapt the laboratory to real-world settings and/or multiple participants (ref). Thirdly, once all the equipment are selected and installed, a major challenge lies in integrating and synchronizing the heterogeneous data streams they produce. Each modality – whether MT, audio, gaze or physiology – is sampled at different rates (with differences in the ranges of 20X), recorded using different hardware and software, and encoded in different formats (ref). Ensuring that all these signals are temporally aligned with sufficient precision and stored in an integrated and accessible format is non-trivial, especially in studies involving many recordings devices in highly naturalistic paradigms with multiple interacting participants. Finally, even after data collection, researchers are faced with the substantial demands of managing and analyzing multi-dimensional, time-varying datasets —such as dozens of 2D video streams, high-resolution audio, and continuous physiological signals—all of which need to be pre-processed, and organized for analysis. Without standardized pipelines or centralized data structures, this process can become fragmented and error-prone, especially when integrating data from multiple participants or sessions (ref).
In most cases, researchers have outsourced these challenges to proprietary companies that manufacture recording systems, software and analyses packages. For instance, when choosing the right equipment to capture participants movements, one might opt for a state-of-the-art MT system from a proprietary company (e.g., such as Vicon or Qualysis) that offers extensive customer support (including installation), optimal recording accuracy, and a user-friendly software with built-in analyses packages (Merriaux et al., 2017). While these proprietary solutions offer clear advantages, they also come with some important drawbacks. In fact, these systems are often prohibitively expensive (e.g., Qualisys: circa 150-200K €, Vicon: 200-250K €) and rely on proprietary licensing (often with monthly subscriptions costs) with closed-sourced software and analyses toolkits (ref). As a result, they are not accessible to many researchers working with limited budgets, nor easily adaptable for use in non-standard experimental setups or in field-based research. Additionally, even when the budget allows, one is still left with the pressing issue of integrating and synchronising motion data with other data streams that themselves might come from different proprietary systems, as each device/software only records its own modality with its specified sampling rate and data format.
Given this context, the field of multimodality is facing a crossroad, or at least faces the challenge to build multiple roads of discovery: on the one hand we could rely primarily on proprietary and expensive systems, or we can invest and build intellectual capital to move towards more affordable and opensource alternatives. Continuing with the former path has clear advantages for well-funded labs that can afford the high costs, but it inevitably excludes under-resourced labs, early-career researchers, or institutions in low- and middle-income countries. Beyond the issue of access, this reliance on closed commercial ecosystems inherently restricts the dissemination of knowledge between the many interdisciplinary groups involved in multimodal research, concentrating the technical expertise behind paywalls and within select manufactures or labs. In contrast, the path of affordable and opensource solutions aims to democratize access to multimodal research, making both the tools and the underlying technical knowledge openly available to anyone interested in using them. This approach has the potential to shape the field into a more equitable, transparent and collaborative scientific ecosystem where researchers engage open pedagogical practices and actively contribute to the development, adaptation, and dissemination of methodological tools.
Here we introduce Mobile Multimodal Laboratory (MMLab). Developed within the Donders institute for Brain, Cognition and Behavior, the MMLab project aims to provide an affordable, open-source solution to anyone interested in capturing multimodal human behaviors in both controlled and ecological environments. It includes suite of freely available resources – that include the present paper, an extensive coding library, and a quarto-based manual – designed to guide users through the process of building a multimodal setup, including synchronizing, recording, and analysing data streams of interest. The MMLab was built around the following key features:
Accessibility: all documentation, code, and tutorials are open sourced to ensure broad accessibility, transparency, and reuse across research communities. Affordability: the proposed setup can be fully assembled for under 10,000€, as it relies on low-cost components and, whenever possible, non-proprietary hardware and software. Portability: MMLab is designed to be compact and easily transportable, allowing researchers to deploy it a range of testing environments beyond traditional lab spaces. Built-in Integration and Synchronization: data from each recording device is centrally integrated through the Lab Streaming Layer (LSL, ref), which allows for precise temporal synchronization of multimodal steams. Modularity: the setup supports a wide range of interchangeable components and sensors compatible with LSL, allowing researchers to customize the lab to suit specific research goals. Adaptability: ?
The present paper serves both as an introductory guide and a step-by-step tutorial designed to walk researchers and technical staff through the process of assembling and operating the MMLab. To illustrate each step, we grounded our guide in a proof-of-concept experiment in which two participants engaged in an interpersonal singing task while being simultaneously recorded across multiple 2D video streams (e.g., for 3D motion tracking), high-frequency microphones (e.g., for prosodic or semantic analyses) and wireless physiological recordings (e.g., ECG, EMG and respiration). All these heterogeneous data streams were integrated and synchronized using the LSL system (ref), an opensource middleware that allows centralized data collection with sub-millisecond synchronization. Our specific experimental configuration is intended as a “default” setup that can be adapted to meet individual research needs and evolving technological capabilities, as other recording devices - such as EEG or eye-tracking – can easily be incorporated into the pipeline, provided they are compatible with the Lab Streaming Layer (LSL). The accompanying coding library and quarto-based manual includes all necessary coding steps and technical details for hardware configuration, synchronization, preprocessing, and multimodal analysis—providing researchers with a complete, ready-to-adapt pipeline.


The tutorial provides a detailed, step-by-step guide on how to (i) set up, (ii) preprocess, and (iii) analyze the multimodal data recorded with the MMLab, grounding these procedures in our proof-of-concept experiment. Following a brief overview of this experimental design, the Methods section is structured into three main parts: Experimental design Setup of the MMLab: This part outlines the specific hardware and software components used in our MMLab, detailing the rationale for choosing our equipment, the steps involved in assembling the components, the recording procedures for each modality, and the integration within the LSL system. Preprocessing of Multimodal Data: This section explains all the steps required to prepare the recorded multimodal data for analysis. Based on the original scripts in our library (ref), here we describe the procedures for extracting data streams from the unified recording file, synchronizing these multimodal streams, and segmenting and clipping data into manageable intervals for subsequent analysis. Multimodal Signal Processing and Analysis. In progess..
Alongside the manuscript, we also provide online manual available at https://multimoblab.github.io/Mobile-Multimodal-Lab/ . The online manual is an extended copy of this manuscript; it provides technical details where necessary and scripts that enable implementions of all steps. Unlike this manuscript, it is meant to be regularly updated to resolve any issues or accommodate wishes of MMLab users.

title: Mobile Multimodal Lab
text: Our proof-of-concept experiment investigates the role of interpersonal synchrony that emerges across multiple modalities (namely vocal output, bodily movements and physiological responses) during a structured singing task. We opted for such paradigm because musical interactions offer a wealth of intra-and-inter-personal dynamics unfolding across different behavioral and physiological channels. For instance, research on music cognition has shown that the perception of and synchronization with musical structure are shaped by multiscale influences, including physiological states (Vickhoff et al., 2013), bodily moments (Toiviainen et al., 2010), psychological traits (Novembre et al., 2019), and processes of musical enculturation (Hannon & Trainor, 2007). This makes it particularly well suited for a mobile multimodal setup that can bring its experimental infrastructure to participants, rather than requiring them to adapt to highly constrained laboratory environments. Crucially, this mobility and multimodality needs to be achieved without sacrificing precision in the recordings, and our MMLab setup enables tightly synchronized recordings at both intra-personal (e.g., heart rate, muscle activity) and inter-personal (e.g., gestural coupling) levels.
MethodsExperimental design Code

1.1 Experimental Rationalle
Our proof-of-concept experiment investigates the role of interpersonal synchrony that emerges across multiple modalities (namely vocalization, bodily movements and physiological markers) during a structured singing task. We opted for such a paradigm because musical interactions offer a wealth of intra-and-inter-personal dynamics unfolding across different behavioral and physiological channels. For instance, research on music cognition has shown that the perception of and synchronization with musical structure are shaped by multiscale influences, including physiological states (Vickhoff et al. 2013), bodily moments (Toiviainen, Luck, and Thompson 2010), psychological traits (Novembre, Mitsopoulos, and Keller 2019), and processes of musical enculturation (Hannon and Trainor 2007). Additionally, at a methodological level, this type of research requires recording of brain/body signals during active behaviors in naturalistic settings. This makes it particularly well suited for a proof-of-concept experiment with the mobile multimodal setup.

1.2 Experimental Design and Procedures
Two participants engaged in a joint singing task within a two-by-two factorial design, manipulating the (1) visual access between participants (Vision vs. NoVision) and the (2) freedom of movement (Movement vs. NoMovement), as depicted in Figure 1A. Each of the four conditions (Vision x Movement, Vision x NoMovement, NoVision x Movement, NoVision x NoMovement) was presented in a random order and consisted of five structured trials: after a keyboard press to initiate the condition and relay the pre-defined marker to the LSL, participants listened to a set of synthetic melodies composed of five randomized MIDI notes that had been created in advance to standardize pitch, duration, and temporal structure. Following the audio presentations, participants were instructed to vocally reproduce the melodies in synchrony with each other during a 10 second interval delimited by start-and-end auditory beeps. A custom Python script handled the presentation of auditory stimuli, the timing of each experimental phase, and the streaming of event markers via LSL.
[Quarto: here is script for presentation of stimuli: MMLab_Stimulus_Presentation_LSL] [SCRIPT: 1_LAB_SETUP/Stimulus/MML_Stimulus_Presentation_LSL.py]
We expected that the Vision_Movement condition would yield the highest levels of vocal synchrony, as visual access and freedom of movement allow participants to couple both motor and vocal-acoustic systems during interaction. However, because this experiment was designed solely to demonstrate the MMLab’s functionality, we did not focus on formal hypothesis testing nor specific outcome measures. Rather, our pipeline was structured such that this placeholder paradigm can be replaced with any experimental design involving one or more participants and two or more data streams.

MethodsOverview Code





Methods Overview
To illustrate each step of the MMLab, we grounded our guide in a proof-of-concept experiment in which two participants engaged in an interpersonal singing task while being simultaneously recorded across multiple 2D video streams (e.g., for 3D motion tracking), high-frequency microphones (e.g., for prosodic or semantic analyses) and wireless physiological sensors capturing electrocardiogram (ECG), electromyography (EMG) and respiration cycles. All these heterogeneous data streams were time-synchronized using the LabStreamingLayer system (LSL, Kothe et al. 2025), an open-source middleware that allows centralized data collection with sub-millisecond synchronization. Our toolkit further offers scripts to handle data integration and processing, and example analysis. This proof-of-concept experimental configuration is intended as the default setup that can be adapted to meet individual research needs and evolving technological capabilities. Other recording devices (e.g., EEG or eye-tracking) can easily be incorporated into the pipeline, provided they are compatible with the LSL.
In the following methods section, we provide a detailed guide on how to (?@sec-setup) set up, (?@sec-preproc) preprocess, (?@sec-process) process, and (?@sec-analysis) analyze the multimodal data recorded with the MMLab setup, grounding these procedures in our (?@sec-exp) proof-of-concept experiment. The methods section is structured into five main parts:

0. The Proof-of-Concept Experiment: This part describes the rationale behind our (?@sec-exp-ratio) experimental paradigm (a structured interpersonal singing task) and (?@sec-exp-design) details of the experimental design and manipulations.


1. Setup of the MMLab: This part outlines the specific hardware and software components used in our MMLab, detailing the rationale for choosing our equipment, the steps involved in assembling the components, and the recording procedures for each modality. Specifically, we describe the setup for video recording optimized for 3D motion tracking (?@sec-setup-video), high-fidelity audio recording (?@sec-setup-audio), wireless physiological recordings of electrocardiogram (ECG), electromyography (EMG) and respiration (?@sec-setup-physio), and the integration and synchronization of all data streams via the LabStreamingLayer (?@sec-setup-lsl).


2. Preprocessing of Multimodal Data: This part details all the steps required to prepare the recorded multimodal data for analysis. Based on our analyses scripts, we describe the procedures for extracting and converting individual streams from the unified recording file (?@sec-preproc-extract), segmenting each stream based on shared LSL timestamps of experimentally relevant events (?@sec-preproc-segment), clipping the externally stored raw videos to match the corresponding LSL time segments (?@sec-preproc-clip), and merging the clipped videos with their synchronized audio recordings (?@sec-preproc-merge).


3. Multimodal Signal Processing: This part details the extraction and filtering of relevant signals from each multimodal time series. We first describe the full motion tracking pipeline (?@sec-process-mt), covering the selection of pose estimation algorithm (?@sec-process-mt-choose), video preparation (?@sec-process-mt-prep), camera calibration (?@sec-process-mt-calib), and 2D and 3D pose estimation via FreeMoCap (?@sec-process-mt-mt). We then describe the signal processing procedures for the remaining modalities (?@sec-process-other), including the extraction of audio amplitude envelopes (?@sec-process-other-audio), ECG filtering (?@sec-process-other-ecg), muscle activation envelopes from EMG (?@sec-process-other-muscleenv), and respiratory waveforms (?@sec-process-other-resp). Finally, we describe how all processed signals are resampled, temporally aligned, and merged into a single multimodal matrix per trial (?@sec-process-merging).


4. Multimodal Analyses: This part presents a proof-of-concept analysis pipeline using mutual information (MI) to quantify interpersonal coupling across modalities and experimental conditions. We describe the signal normalization procedures (?@sec-analysis-norm) and the MI analysis framework (?@sec-analysis-mi), including time-lagged and sliding-window computations across all between-participant signal pairs.








References

Kothe, Christian, Seyed Yahya Shirazi, Tristan Stenner, David Medine, Chadwick Boulay, Matthew I. Grivich, Fiorenzo Artoni, Tim Mullen, Arnaud Delorme, and Scott Makeig. 2025. “The Lab Streaming Layer for Synchronized Multimodal Recording.” Imaging Neuroscience 3: IMAG.a.136. https://doi.org/10.1162/IMAG.a.136.
MethodsMotion tracking Code

1.1 Motion Tracking

1.1.1 Choosing the Motion Tracking Software
Extracting motion data from standard RGB videos requires a pose estimation model - i.e., a computer vision model, typically built on convolutional or transformer neural networks, that has been pre-trained on large annotated datasets to localize landmarks in human bodies (e.g., shoulders, elbows, wrists, etc.) in each video frame (Voulodimos et al. 2018). Over the last decade, several freely available (and mostly open-source) pose estimation libraries have been developed, including OpenPose (Cao et al. 2021), MediaPipe (Lugaresi et al. 2019), DeepLabCut (Mathis et al. 2018), and, more recently, large “foundation” models such as Sapiens (Khirodkar et al. 2025).
These libraries primarily output 2D keypoints from each camera view (although some do provide a monocular 3D estimate, but these estimates are not metrically accurate and are generally unsuitable for quantitative biomechanical analysis). Therefore, obtaining research-grade 3D coordinates requires combining 2D detections from multiple (typically 3 or more) synchronized cameras with a geometric triangulation step based on camera calibration parameters (intrinsic and extrinsic), analogous to how device-based motion capture systems reconstruct 3D positions from their marker detections.
For the MMLab, we aimed to find a motion tracking pipeline that adheres to our standards of accessibility, affordability and modularity. Additionally, we aimed for wrapping all steps (namely pose estimation, camera calibration, and 3D triangulation) into a single, reproducible pipeline, thus making it accessible to researchers without a specialized computer vision or biomechanics background. Therefore, we chose FreeMocap (Cherian, Idehen, and Matthis 2023), an open-source motion tracking pipeline that integrates both 2D and 3D tracking into a single, Python-based workflow using an intuitive graphical interface for user accessibility. FreeMoCap uses the MediaPipe Holistic model to detect 2D landmarks on the whole body (33 points), with added (option) face (up to 468 points) and hands (21 points per hand) from each synchronized camera view, and then uses Anipose (Karashchuk et al., 2021) to triangulate these 2D detections into 3D coordinates (in meters). Detailed instructions on how to set up and use FreeMoCap can be found here.
Below, we describe the steps we employed to prepare the videos and calibrate the cameras to perform motion tracking with FreeMoCap. An Overview of these preparatory steps and motion tracking pipeline can be seen in Figure 3.


1.1.2 Video Preparation
FreeMoCap expects each camera view to be provided as a separate, time-aligned video file. Since we recorded each triplet of cameras as a single composite file (?@sec-setup-video), we first split each composite recording into three individual videos using a custom Python script built around the OpenCV library
[Quarto Link with Script and Explanation MML_Video_Split.ipynb] For each (trimmed) video recording (obtained in ?@sec-preproc-clip), the script reads the video stream frame by frame, retrieves the native resolution and frame rate from the OpenCV metadata, and slices each frame horizontally into three equal-width sections corresponding to the three camera views. [CODE: 3_MOTION_TRACKING/1_Video_Segmentation/MML_Video_Split.ipynb#video-split-setup] These sections are then written out as three separate video files that preserve the original frame rate and inherit the synchronization of the source recording. Both the output codec/container and the assumed number of cameras per source file are parameterized, allowing the script to be reused for setups with different recording configurations.


1.1.3 Camera Calibration
In order to reconstruct 3D coordinates from the 2D landmarks, we computed intrinsic and extrinsic parameters of each camera trio from the ChArUco board calibration videos (see ?@sec-setup-video) using the Anipose library (Karashchuk et al. 2021).
[Quarto Link with Script and Explanation MMLab_Calibration_anipose.ipynb] The script iterates through the output of the previous splitting step and bundles together the three corresponding videos (from each session). Aniposelib then processes this three-video bundle by detecting the ChArUco markers in every frame and matching corresponding detections across the synchronized videos, solving jointly for the intrinsic matrix of each camera and the extrinsic transformations between them. The board parameters used in this script are specific to our physical calibration target (i.e., a 7 × 5 ChArUco board with 108-mm squares and 85-mm ArUco markers drawn from the default 4 × 4-bit dictionary of 50 patterns), and should be adjusted by the user if a differently sized board is used. [CODE: 3_MOTION_TRACKING/2_Video_Calibration/MMLab_Calibration_anipose.ipynb#calib-board] The resulting calibration parameters are then written into a TOML file for each session. [CODE: 3_MOTION_TRACKING/2_Video_Calibration/MMLab_Calibration_anipose.ipynb#calib-anipose-run] Ideally, average reprojection error is less than 1 pixel (but acceptable until 3 pixels, see Karashchuk et al., 2021)


1.1.4 Motion Tracking and Triangulation
The three split video and the corresponding TOML calibration parameters were then passed to FreeMoCap which performed two sequential operations. Firstly, it ran the MediaPipe’s Holistic model on each of the three videos to localize, frame by frame, the coordinates of the anatomical landmarks in the 2D pixel space for the whole body (head, torso, arms, legs, and feet, 33 keypoints in total) and hands (21 keypoints per hand). Secondly, these 2D keypoints were triangulated into 3D world coordinates using Anipose, based on the precomputed calibration parameters, yielding x, y and z positions (in meters, relative to the camera rig) for each landmark in each frame. To reduce high-frequency jitter, we also applied a 4th-order, zero-phase Butterworth filter with a 7-Hz cutoff to both the 2D and 3D trajectories, leveraging FreeMoCap’s post-processing stage. Because FreeMoCap returns one sample per video frame, the resulting 2D and 3D landmark time series have the effective frame rate of each recording (i.e., the rate at which the cameras actually delivered frames, nominally 60 fps, see ?@sec-preproc-clip). These time series were saved as CSV files (for details on the FreeMoCap workflow, see the documentation). Since webcam frame rates are not perfectly constant, we did not assume a fixed sampling rate. Instead, each frame was assigned its corresponding LSL timestamp when merging the motion data with the other modalities (Section 1.3). Although FreeMoCap outputs the full set of whole-body and hand landmarks, for the proof-of-concept coupling analyses presented in ?@sec-analysis we carried forward only the right index finger landmark (x, y, z axes) into the merged multimodal dataset (see Section 1.3), as the right hand motion was the most salient movement during our co-singing task.

1.2 Other Multimodal Signals Processing
To extract and filter the signals from audio and physiological time series, we used a single python script that iterates through the inputs, identifies the relevant files, applies the modality-specific processing pipeline, and merges all signals together (per trial) in a csv file.
[Quarto Link with Script and Explanation MMLab_Multimodal_Filtering.ipynb] The script is built around the librosa (McFee et al., 2015) and SciPy (Virtanen et al., 2020) libraries and contains two general-purpose filtering methods that are used across all modalities. The first is a butterworth filter, which can be flexibly implemented as a low-pass, high-pass or bandpass filter depending on the analyses. All Butterworth filters are applied with zero-phase (forward–backward) filtering (via scipy.signal.filtfilt), which eliminates the phase distortion that a single-pass filter would introduce. To prevent boundary artefacts, each signal is padded with 1000 edge-replicated samples before filtering and trimmed back to its original length afterwards. [CODE: 4a_PROCESSED/Script_FILTERING/MML_Multimodal_Filtering.ipynb#filter-butterworth] All high-pass, low-pass, and bandpass filters described in the subsections below use this same Butterworth design unless otherwise noted. The second is a notch filter (via scipy.signal.iirnotch), which is used to suppress narrowband electrical interferences acquired during recordings (in our case, the European grid frequency of 50 Hz). The sharpness of the notch is controlled by a quality factor (Q), where higher values produce a narrower rejection band (we used Q = 30 throughout, which removes the 50-Hz component with minimal distortion of neighbouring frequencies). [CODE: 4a_PROCESSED/Script_FILTERING/MML_Multimodal_Filtering.ipynb#filter-notch]

1.2.1 Audio Amplitude Envelope
From each raw audio time-series, we extracted a smoothed amplitude envelope from the audio, which represents the slowly-varying time-series tracking instantaneous loudness and capturing the rhythmic structure of the participants’ vocalizations. To do so, we followed a similar procedure outlined by Tilsen and Arvaniti (2013). First, the denoised mono audio (sampled at 16 kHz) was filtered with a 2nd-order zero-phase Butterworth bandpass spanning 400–4000 Hz (i.e., a sequential high-pass and low-pass filter). This bandpass filtering isolates the frequency range that carries most of the vocal energy (fundamental frequencies and harmonics of the sung voice) while removing low-frequency rumble (e.g., HVAC noise, microphone handling, breath sounds) and high-frequency hiss. Second, the bandpassed signal was rectified by taking its absolute value, converting the oscillating waveform into its instantaneous magnitude. Third, the rectified signal was smoothed with a 2nd-order zero-phase Butterworth low-pass filter at 10 Hz, preserving the note- and phrase-level amplitude modulations of interest while attenuating faster fluctuations within individual notes. Fourth, the resulting envelope was min–max normalized to the [0, 1] range, thus resulting in a scale-invariant signal comparable across recordings and within participants.
[Plot of Raw and Cleaned Audio for Quarto] Figure S7. Plot of Raw (Blue) and Filtered (Blue) Audio Signal.


1.2.2 ECG Filtering
To filter the raw ECG signal (sampled at 1 kHz), we first applied a 4th-order high-pass filter at 0.5 Hz to remove slow baseline drifts caused by respiration and electrode motion, followed by a 4th-order low-pass filter at 20 Hz to attenuate high-frequency muscle artefacts. We then applied a notch filter centered at 50 Hz (Q = 30) to suppress grid-frequency electrical interference picked up by the sensor cables. Following visual inspection of these signals, we decided to apply an additional denoising step using the Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD, Huang et al. 1998), a data-driven method that decomposes a signal into a series of oscillatory components (Intrinsic Mode Functions, or IMFs) ordered from highest to lowest frequency. We extracted and discarded the first IMF, which captures the fastest residual oscillations that were not fully removed by the Butterworth filters, and retained the second IMF as the cleaned ECG signal. This EMD step was implemented using the emd package (Quinn et al. 2021). Note, this deviates from gold-standard signal ECG processing pipelines to some extent, as our aim was to retrieve a smooth cardiac signal reflecting the heart cycle dynamics rather than to process the time series to estimate heart rate intervals (e.g., for heart rate variability).
[Plot of Raw and Cleaned ECG for Quarto]
Figure S8. Plot of Raw (grey) and Filtered (blue) ECG signal.


1.2.3 Muscle Activation Envelopes
The raw EMG signals from the biceps and triceps sensors (sampled at 1K Hz) were processed in three steps to obtain a smoothed muscle activation envelope. Firstly, a 4th-order high-pass filter at 30 Hz removed low-frequency artefacts such as movement-related baseline shifts and any residual cardiac contamination. Secondly, the high-passed signal was full-wave rectified (absolute value), converting the bipolar EMG bursts into a unipolar magnitude signal. Thirdly, a 4th-order low-pass filter at 20 Hz smoothed the rectified signal into a continuous activation envelope that tracks the overall contraction intensity of the muscle over time. This high-pass, rectify-low, pass sequence is a standard approach for extracting linear envelopes from surface EMG (e.g., De Luca et al. 2010; Pouw et al. 2025). Both the biceps and triceps envelopes were processed identically and saved as separate columns in the output CSV.
[Plot of Raw and Cleaned EMG for Quarto]
Figure S9. Plot of Raw (grey) and Filtered (blue) EMG signals for Bicep (top) and Tricep (bottom)


1.2.4 Respiratory Envelope
The raw respiration signal (sampled at 1 kHz) was smoothed with a 4th-order low-pass filter at 1 Hz to isolate the slow respiratory waveform and remove high-frequency noise from the piezoelectric sensor. The resulting continuous time series the cyclical inhalation and exhalation cycles rather than very finescale fluctuations in chest kinematics.
[Plot of Raw and Cleaned Resp for Quarto]

1.3 Multimodal Signal Merging
The final processing step merges all the individual filtered signals into a single, time-aligned multimodal matrix, which is necessary for the cross-modal coupling analyses described in ?@sec-analysis. This requires resolving two challenges inherent to multimodal recordings. First, each modality operates at its native sampling rate – 60 Hz for the motion tracking (the frame rate of the Elgato Facecams), 16 kHz for the audio amplitude envelope, and 1 kHz for the physiological signals (ECG, EMGs, RESP). Second, even signals sharing a nominal sampling rate carry different timestamps, because LSL timestamps reflect the precise moment each sample arrived at the receiving machine, which varies across devices due to differences in internal buffering, and transmission latencies (for more information see here). Additionally, the motion tracking output from FreeMoCap is indexed by video frame numbers, which need to be mapped to their corresponding LSL timestamps.
To address this, the script performs three operations:


time-zeros each stream and maps motion frame indices to LSL timestamps;


[CODE: 4a_PROCESSED/Script_FILTERING/MML_Multimodal_Filtering.ipynb#merge-frame-to-lsl]


resamples all modalities to a 1 kHz vector using linear interpolation (whereby prior low-pass filtering perfomed in Section 1.2 prevents resampling artefacts);


[CODE: 4a_PROCESSED/Script_FILTERING/MML_Multimodal_Filtering.ipynb#merge-time-grid]
